gap: No result ChatGPT got states that MonsGeek's own FAQ limits the FUN60 (and M1 V5 TMR) to N-pole-down magnetic switches and says S-pole-down switches "will not function properly", so the hot-swap these boards advertise depends on the magnet's orientation.
standout_why: Compared against PCWorld, Notebookcheck, MKB Guide, keyboardtester.click and HLPlanet (all opened 2026-11-26); the RTINGS 60% page only names the FUN60 Ultra in a link list. PCWorld and Notebookcheck say the TMR version takes 5-pin mechanical switches but never mention magnet polarity. MKB Guide gives a north-pole-down limit only for the Hall effect Epomaker HE60, and says just "compatible magnetic switches" for the FUN60 Ultra TMR. keyboardtester.click has no polarity content. HLPlanet's explainer says sensing is in-plane and magnet position differs, with power figures, but gives no pole rule for any board. None quotes Wooting's point that most TMR sensors sit off-axis and need signal boosting.
decides: It does not change the performance ranking; it confirms that TMR by itself is not the reason to pick one board, since Wooting says firmware and software decide accuracy once sensor noise is set aside. It does decide whether a switch-swap plan works: on the FUN60 Ultra only N-pole-down magnetic switches work, and mechanical switches fit only the TMR-sensor variant. On our Gamakay TK75 TMR, HLPlanet says a key with a mechanical switch needs rapid trigger turned off or it can double-click, and release settings below about 0.3 mm can misread on neighbouring keys. TMR's lower sensor draw did not give the FUN60 long 8K wireless runtime (Notebookcheck: about 3 hours with LEDs on 4,000 mAh), which favours the TK75 TMR's 8,000 mAh battery for wireless buyers. The TK75 TMR is under $100 only at its sale price of $89.99.

findings.label: Magnet pole the board accepts (maker FAQ)
findings.value: "These models only support N-pole-down magnetic switches." "S-pole-down switches will not function properly with these models."
findings.source_title: MonsGeek FAQ: Compatible magnetic switches for M1 V5 TMR and FUN60
findings.note: The FAQ covers the M1 V5 TMR and FUN60 models. The answer carries no date. It does not mention mechanical switches.

findings.label: Magnetic switches MonsGeek names as N-pole-down examples
findings.value: AKKO Windy / Glare / Astrolink; Gateron Jade / Jade Pro / Jade Gaming; TTC Uranus / TTC King ("such as (but not limited to)")
findings.source_title: MonsGeek FAQ: Compatible magnetic switches for M1 V5 TMR and FUN60
findings.note: Maker's list, not a test. See "unsourced" for a possible conflict with MonsGeek's Astrolink FAQ that was not opened.

findings.label: Mechanical-switch swap (MagMech) by sensor variant, and a named incompatible switch
findings.value: MagMech: "Supported (TMR Sensor)" / "Not Supported (HE Sensor)"; 5-pin mechanical hot-swap "for TMR Version only"; Akko Magnetic Creamy Yellow "use a downward-facing S-pole magnet" and "are not compatible with the FUN60"
findings.note: Maker's product page. It also states 8000Hz polling "in wired or 2.4G wireless modes", RT accuracy 0.01-2.00mm, and a 4000mAh battery on the tri-mode version only. It gives no Bluetooth polling rate and no battery-life figure.

findings.label: Price on the maker's US page
findings.value: $69.99 – $89.99 (range across the FUN60 Ultra variants; no per-variant price read)
findings.note: The page showed only the range, with options Tri-mode (ANSI) and USB-C Wired (ANSI). With no variant chosen the buy button read "Unavailable" with "Join Waitlist". It also carried the notice "Pre-orders for the FUN60 Ultra HE Wired are expected to ship around the 23th." The TMR variant's exact price and stock were not confirmed; monsgeek.com is not a Shopify store, so storecheck failed on it.

findings.label: 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth battery life (named reviewer)
findings.value: About 3 hours at 2.4 GHz with the LEDs lit; about 4 to 5 hours in Bluetooth; 4,000 mAh battery
findings.source_title: MonsGeek Fun60 Ultra TMR hands-on review - Notebookcheck
findings.note: Notebookcheck adds that the driver offers no way to lower the polling rate to stretch runtime. PCWorld (https://www.pcworld.com/article/3014690/monsgeek-fun60-ultra-review.html, read 2026-11-26) says 8K wireless with RGB "often only lasted a few hours" and "the battery lasts for days" on Bluetooth or dimmed lighting. The two reviewers disagree on Bluetooth runtime.

findings.label: How TMR sensors sit under the switch, in Wooting's words
findings.value: "Most TMR sensors are mounted off-axis, which increases signal interference and requires higher sensitivity to compensate." TMR sensors "do require signal boosting to work in a keyboard."
findings.source_title: Hall Effect vs TMR: Pause the funeral - Wooting
findings.note: Post dated 27 May 2026, author Jedidiah. Wooting sells Hall effect keyboards, so this is a competitor's position. It adds that Hall effect sensors "and some recent TMR sensors" have adopted vertical (Z-axis) placement.

findings.label: Sensor power draw, TMR vs Hall effect (Wooting's testing)
findings.value: "TMR sensors consumed 5 to 10 times less power than Hall Effect sensors after signal boosting."
findings.source_title: Hall Effect vs TMR: Pause the funeral - Wooting
findings.note: Wooting gives no mA figures. HLPlanet's explainer (https://www.hlplanet.com/tmr-vs-hall-effect-sensors/, read 2026-11-26) lists Hall 5-10 mA vs TMR 0.001-0.01 mA with no source; that is a far larger ratio than Wooting's 5-10x.

findings.label: What limits accuracy once sensor noise is set aside (Wooting)
findings.value: "Outside of sensor noise, firmware and software become the biggest factors for accuracy and precision." "TMR is a genuinely interesting technology, but it hasn't taken the lead in either performance or stability."
findings.source_title: Hall Effect vs TMR: Pause the funeral - Wooting
findings.note: Also: "Pre-2020s Hall Effect sensors had measurably worse noise performance than TMR sensors, but that gap has largely closed." and "Even something as small as a switch's magnet size can change your accuracy and need a software update."

findings.label: Mechanical switches and rapid trigger on the same board (named reviewer)
findings.value: "accepts 5-pin mechanical switches"; rapid trigger should be turned off on any key holding a mechanical switch, "otherwise double-click behavior can occur"
findings.note: Review dated May 18, 2026, when the price was $119.99. It names only Mercury V3 and Phoenix V3 Silent as magnetic switches and does not state a magnet pole. Software is the Gear Hub/Lab web app at gearhub.top.

findings.label: False releases at low rapid-trigger settings (named reviewer)
findings.value: Below about 0.3 mm release, firm presses can flex the plate and "the sensors can misread as a release event on neighboring keys"; HLPlanet suggests about 0.4 mm
findings.note: The spec sheet lists rapid trigger at "0.01 mm precision". HLPlanet says light typists are unlikely to see the problem.

findings.label: Polling rate by connection and battery (named reviewer)
findings.note: HLPlanet could not fully deplete the battery and gives no runtime. 8,000 mAh is twice the FUN60 Ultra's 4,000 mAh (8,000 / 4,000 = 2); that is capacity, not measured runtime.
